On the Sources and the Title

The present work, titled Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah, draws upon a number of classical sources within the broader literature of Islamic spiritual sciences. Its primary foundations are derived from Imām Aḥmad al-Būnī's Shams al-Maʿārif al-Kubrā and Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah, two works that have long served as important references for the study of Divine Names, letter symbolism (ʿilm al-ḥurūf), invocations, correspondences, and spiritual practices associated with the Būnian tradition. Additional material has been informed by collections such as Majmūʿat al-Aḥzāb, which preserves devotional formulas and litanies transmitted through the spiritual heritage, as well as Uṣūl al-Basṭfī Sirr al-Awfāq wa al-Ḥawāṣṣ.

The title Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah was chosen deliberately. It does not imply that this work replaces, reproduces, or claims the authority of the original texts from which it draws. Rather, it reflects the intention of the compiler: to present a focused recension of selected foundational principles (uṣūl) underlying these sciences, arranged according to the themes and areas of emphasis most relevant to the intended reader. In this sense, the title refers not to a new claim of authorship, but to a gathering (compilation) of essential foundations of wisdom (ḥikmah) drawn from a wider inherited tradition.
Iḥyāʾ Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah
The Revival of the Foundations of Wisdom
Compiled by: Amin Patel
Dedication
This work is dedicated —

Foreword
Knowledge is of many kinds. There is knowledge that informs the

mind, knowledge that disciplines the limbs, and knowledge that purifies the heart. The scholars of every generation have distinguished between these forms of knowledge, for confusing their purposes can lead sincere seekers away from the path intended for them.

Among the inherited sciences of Islam is what later generations came to call ʿilm al-rūḥāniyyāt, the spiritual sciences concerned with the Divine Names, Qurʾanic invocations, healing, protection, and the subtle realities of creation. Like all sacred sciences, it has its etiquette (adab), its people, its chains of transmission (isnād), and its conditions. It was never intended to be pursued without discipline, guidance, and proper preparation.

This recension of the works of Imām Aḥmad al-Būnī is therefore a welcome contribution. Throughout the history of our spiritual traditions, knowledge was received through companionship, instruction, and authorization. Books preserve the memory of a tradition, but teachers preserve its understanding.

The seeker must therefore approach these sciences with humility. The opening of a manuscript is not the opening of a path. A text may describe methods and principles, but it cannot replace the guidance of those who have inherited the responsibility of teaching and correcting the seeker.

Our masters of taṣawwuf have always emphasized that extraordinary experiences are not the measure of spiritual attainment. Visions, unveilings, and unusual phenomena are secondary matters. The true fruit of the path is sincerity before Allah, purification of the heart, beautiful character, and service to creation. If the pursuit of rūḥāniyyāt assists these aims, it becomes a means of benefit; if it distracts from them, it becomes a veil.

The compiler, Amin Patel, has devoted years to the study and practice of rūḥāniyyāt under multiple teachers and, having received idhn in this discipline, has served his community as a practitioner of spiritual healing. In preparing this recension, he has rendered a valuable service by making these foundational materials freely available to serious students. Yet every reader should remember that no book can grant idhn, nor can written knowledge replace companionship with the people of Allah.

Imām al-Būnī occupies a distinguished place within the history of the Islamic spiritual sciences. He belonged to a civilisation in which scholarship, spirituality, and disciplined apprenticeship were inseparable. Traditional Sufi accounts also place him within the same broader Maghribī intellectual milieu as Shaykh Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn ʿArabī, with both associated through their inheritance of ʿilm al-ḥurūf with the teaching of Shaykh ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Mahdawī. Their works represent different expressions of a living tradition in which the outward and inward sciences were cultivated together under qualified masters.

Although this work draws from Shams al-Maʿārif and Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah, it should be approached as a reference and companion to those works, not as a substitute for living instruction. The sciences of the spirit are preserved not only through books, but through sound intention, righteous companionship, and responsible transmission.

To those beginning this journey: rectify the apparent before seeking the hidden. Establish worship before seeking unveilings. Purify intention before seeking influence. If Allah has written a portion of these sciences for you, He will open the appropriate doors through the means He has chosen.
May Allah Most High grant us beneficial knowledge, protect us from knowledge that increases arrogance, illuminate our hearts with sincerity, and make every step a means of drawing nearer to Him.
Syed Hamza Jalalpuri
Servant of the Chishti Path
Introduction
The first edition of this work was completed in early 2021 as a highly

abridged synthesis of two of the most influential works of Shaykh Aḥmad al-Būnī: Shams al-Maʿārif and Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah, and was released on the internet through various channels for free. The present edition, released in 2026, is substantially revised and expanded. While retaining the original aim of providing a practical reference to the foundational concepts of the Būnian tradition, it incorporates additional material, editorial refinements, and a deeper appreciation.

This work should not be mistaken for a curriculum of spiritual training. Like the classical texts from which it draws, it is intended as a reference rather than a manual capable of replacing a qualified teacher. The literature of rūḥāniyyāt has always functioned in conjunction with living transmission (talqīn), authorization (idhn), and disciplined practice and riyadah under appropriate guidance. Detached from that context, even the most celebrated texts reveal only part of the tradition they seek to preserve. Errors and misdirection in the manuscript, both deliberate and unintended are part and parcel of rūḥāniyyāt literature.

Looking back upon my own journey, I have come to appreciate that one does not simply choose the path of rūḥāniyyāt; rather, one finds oneself drawn toward it. Within qadar, there are paths that appear to open naturally for some while remaining closed to others despite sincere effort. The aspirant ultimately discovers that advancement in this discipline depends upon Divine permission before it depends upon personal determination.

For those who are also travellers upon the path of sulūk under the guidance of a kāmil shaykh, the extent to which the sciences of rūḥāniyyāt are cultivated is likewise governed by that spiritual training. Different ṭuruq have historically adopted different attitudes toward extraordinary spiritual phenomena such as kashf and other forms of unveiling. Some regard such experiences as secondary or even distracting when compared with the higher objective of attaining proximity to Allah through purification of the soul. Where one's teachers discourage such pursuits, wisdom lies in following their direction rather than attempting to force openings that do not belong to one's path.

My own rūḥāniyyāt teachers have been many, some living and others now departed. Throughout that journey, it is striking that the foundational texts of the thirteenth century were never employed as teaching manuals, not even once. Although works such as Shams al-Maʿārif and Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah remain indispensable historical and intellectual landmarks, they function principally as repositories of principles, correspondences, and inherited methods. They were never intended to substitute for apprenticeship. Every student's development unfolds differently, often in a manner that is neither predictable nor linear.

Like taṣawwuf itself, rūḥāniyyāt is best understood as a living tradition rather than a closed historical system. One may reasonably view it as a specialized sub-branch within the broader framework of taṣawwuf, cultivated only by certain disciples according to aptitude, temperament, and the judgement of their teachers. Its purpose is not the pursuit of marvels (karāmāt) or extraordinary experiences for their own sake. The true aim of sulūk has always been maʿrifat Allāh, the experiential knowledge of Allah. Nevertheless, every community requires individuals capable of healing, spiritual counsel, and other specialized forms of service (khidma), and it is within this sphere that the disciplined study of rūḥāniyyāt has traditionally found its place, under a licensed mentor.

The methods preserved in al-Būnī's writings represent, in many respects, the technical vocabulary and operative conventions of their age. They remain invaluable for understanding the historical foundations of the discipline, yet no living tradition remains frozen in the century of its earliest texts. As generations of teachers inherit, refine, and transmit knowledge, methods evolve while remaining rooted in the same spiritual principles. Contemporary practitioners therefore inherit not only books but living chains of transmission (asānīd), practical disciplines (riyāḍāt), periods of retreat (khalwah), and authorizations received through their teachers.

Within many lineages, teachers speak of instruction received through the broader spiritual inheritance of their silsilah, whether through the fellowship of the righteous, the unseen company associated with their order and hadra, or souls from the alam al arwah, in some instances through the Ḥaḍrah al-Muḥammadiyyah, reserved for the elect adepts. Such matters belong to the experiential vocabulary of the tradition itself and cannot be authenticated or transmitted by books alone. They remain inseparable from the teacher-disciple relationship and from the ethical and spiritual disciplines that accompany it. The tradition is not “reconstructed” from books, ours, the rūḥāniyyāt tradion is a living one. One requires an inner and an outer contact. Let it be known that the path of a rūḥāniyyāt adept is not an easy one.

For this reason, no book can confer idhn. Authorization belongs to those qualified to grant it. Nor should this compilation be regarded as offering spiritual protection, practical competency, or permission to engage in practices that have traditionally required supervision. Those who pursue these sciences without appropriate guidance do so entirely upon their own responsibility, and at great personal risk, at times, irreversable.

Likewise, readers whose own ṭarīqah or teachers discourage the study of rūḥāniyyāt are encouraged to honour that guidance. Fidelity to one's shaykh and one's path takes precedence over curiosity. Every tradition possesses its own pedagogy and priorities, and spiritual progress is better served through obedience than through indiscriminate accumulation of knowledge.

This compilation has therefore been prepared simply as an act of khidmah: a freely offered reference for serious students (with a mentor) who may benefit from having in one compilation, a carefully selected recension of two foundational works. It is intended to accompany learning, not replace it; to illuminate principles, not confer mastery.

In the end, the sciences of rūḥāniyyāt, however subtle or profound, remain secondary to the greater journey. Where the path of rūḥāniyyāt reaches its horizon, the path of sulūk has, in many respects, only just begun. May we not get sidelined by “sidequests”.

May Allah grant every sincere seeker what is best for them, open the doors that are beneficial, close those that are harmful, and, if it is written in their decree, allow them to cross the threshold into these sciences with wisdom, humility, and sound guidance. Āmīn.
Amin Patel,
Ottawa, Canada
4 August 2026

Prologue — The Conditions and Practice of This Science

[I 7] The Conditions and Practice of This Science The conditions of this science are founded upon the basic principles laid down by the scholars, and if these conditions are not observed, the workings performed will not come to pass. The secrets of Allah, the Exalted, lie in His letters, His names, and His noble verses, and He bestows these secrets upon His righteous servants. Indeed Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, declares this in the Noble Qur'an, Sūrat Ghafir (al-Mu'min), verse 60:
(Worship and call upon Me, that I may answer you)

There are certain conditions for working with this science of khawāṣṣ, and so long as these conditions are not fulfilled, a working that is carried out will never come to pass. The conditions of this blessed science are as follows:
1. Firm resolve: Never doubt a working that you are about to perform, for doubt spoils the working that is done. Our Prophet, Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), said:
(Call upon Allah while certain that your
prayer will be answered.) In accordance with this noble hadith, one must begin the working with perfect faith and turn to Allah, Glorious is His Majesty, believing with the heart.

2. Patience: Without growing bored, tired, or weary, one must continue with full patience and concentration until the work one has begun ends in success. Allah, the Exalted, declares in the Noble Qur'an:

[I 8] (O you who believe! Be patient, and vie with one another in patience, and bind yourselves with your whole being to Allah, may He be glorified and exalted. And fear Allah, that you may attain salvation. Sūrat Āl 'Imrān, verse 200.)
For he who strives attains his goal, and every one who strives has his portion. Our Prophet, Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), said:
He who is patient attains victory.
3. Keeping the secret: You must tell no one, and let no one sense, what you are about to do, what you are reciting, or what work you are engaged in. Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

(Seek help in the fulfillment of your needs by keeping your secret.) Perform the working in a secluded place where no one can see you. Never say to anyone, "I did such and such," or "I do such and such!" The saying of Hazrat Omer (may Allah be pleased with him), "He who keeps his secret is safe from harm," is well known.
4. Being God-fearing: Rising on the spiritual path and attaining success come through piety and God-consciousness (takva), for Allah declares in Sūrat Tā-Hā, verse 132:
(A good end is attained through piety.)

This means not eating what is forbidden, eating and drinking only what is lawful, avoiding and refraining from backbiting, not lying, giving importance to truthfulness and sincere counsel, not looking upon others with an evil eye, not tormenting people while bearing torment oneself, and looking upon people with compassion and mercy.

5. Not being hasty: Perform the working you intend to do without haste, with tranquility of heart, free from every thought in your mind (family, wealth, [I 9] joy, fear, grief, and the like), gathering your strength, your resolve (himma), your will, and your desire upon a single point, so that your aim may be fulfilled. Do the work you undertake with love and willingness. No good comes of work done carelessly, as a mere formality.

6. Being clean: You must be in a constant state of ritual purity, and pay great attention to the cleanliness of your body, your clothing, and the place where you are and above all, the cleanliness of your heart.
7. Being licensed: It is essential that the person carrying out this work hold an icazet (a master's authorization). A person without icazet is like a fatherless child.

8. Identifying: When you wish to perform a working of love, attraction, separation, affliction, spirit-sending, summoning, causing illness, healing the sick, or the like upon someone, you identify — that is, come to know — that person's complexion, appearance, height, and whether they are old or young. If you do not know these things, you write using the name of the person's mother instead. If you do not know the mother's name either, you take it to be Havva (Eve) and write accordingly. Identification is more effective than merely giving a name, and more effective still is to use identification and names together.

9. Practicing ascetic discipline (riyada): One must not eat the meat of animals or animal products such as milk, honey, and eggs, nor onions, garlic, or foods of similarly foul odor, and the stomach must be neither empty nor stuffed to excess.
10. Having spiritual resolve (himma): Do not make a tool of exalted things for base purposes! For Allah, the Exalted, declares in Sūrat al-Baqara, verse 41:
(Do not sell My verses for a paltry price.) Do not use the verses of Allah, the Exalted, for evil deeds or evil intentions!

11. Knowing the time of the working: Determine carefully the day and hour of the working to be performed, in accordance with the properties of the planets. Furthermore, the day of the working must not be an inauspicious day. In every lunar month, the 3rd, 5th, 13th, 16th, 21st, 24th, and 25th days are inauspicious days. Do not perform beneficial workings on these menkut days! Beneficial workings should be done on the days when the light of the moon is increasing, while harmful workings should be done on the days when the moon is waning [I 10] (the last three nights of every lunar month).
12. Facing the qibla: When performing a working, write while facing the qibla, the direction of prayer toward Mecca. Arrange the writing according to the original and place each element correctly.

If the writing is a name or a noble verse, a word or letter that comes later must not be moved earlier, nor may a word or letter that comes earlier be moved later. Moreover, the handwriting must be very fine. If a wafq is being written, the numbers or letters must be placed according to the order of the wafq's cells, the numbers or letters must be written beautifully, and the cells of the wafq must be drawn equal to one another.

13. Invoking blessings upon the Prophet: Before and after every working, invoke the noble salawat upon Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him). Our Prophet, Muḥammad Mustafa (peace and blessings be upon him), said on this matter:
(A supplication made between two salawat is never turned away.)
The following blessed salawat is highly meritorious:

(O Allah, send blessings upon our master and liege-lord Muḥammad, the Prophet, and upon his family and Companions, and grant them peace — blessings as numerous as Your creation, as pleasing to You, as heavy as Your Throne, and as abundant as the ink of Your words.)

14. Istikhara: If you perform the istikhara prayer before every working, you will act with insight in the work you undertake. The istikhara is performed as follows: you pray two rak'ahs. In the first rak'ah you recite al-Fātiḥa together with Sūrat al-Kafirun, and in the second rak'ah al-Fātiḥa together with Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ; after giving the salam, you recite the following istikhara supplication three, five, or seven times. The istikhara supplication to be recited is this:
I 11] (... ḥājati) — In the phrase written within]) .the parentheses, you insert whatever your need actually is

(O God, I seek Your guidance through Your knowledge, and I seek ability through Your power, and I ask of You from Your immense bounty, that You make plain to me the outcome of this matter — of such-and-such a thing, and here he mentions his need. If it is good for me, then open my breast to it and grant me success in accomplishing it; and if it is bad, then turn it away from me and turn me away from it, for You have power over all things.)
If you find ease and peace in your heart, you carry out the working (amal) believing that you will succeed in it and reach your goal.

But if your spirit feels constricted, you abandon it. Persisting anyway will only work to your harm. The istihare (the prayer for divine guidance) must be performed fully awake and with the heart believing in the power of God Most High, for He alone knows the truth of things and how they will end.

15. Not employing the spirits (ruhaniyyun) in base tasks: If you try to employ the spirits for base and unworthy works, you will have insulted and demeaned them. Because the spirits act according to the Sacred Law (sheriat), they will not carry out any working that is doubtful. Never attempt to employ them in matters contrary to the Sacred Law! Also, do not go asking the spirits about every need you have.

Memorizing the azaim (conjuration formulas): The azaim you will recite to the spirits (rūḥāniyya) must also be memorized thoroughly, and you must not stammer at all while reciting them. It is not enough to read the ʿazīma from a book or from a tablet (lawḥ), for then the heart becomes occupied with the writing and the necessary reverent absorption (hushu') is lost. This in turn removes concentrated attention (tewejjuh), which is the most essential of the pillars (erkan) of the working.

17. How the working is carried out: If, in a working you undertake, you need to write upon a tablet (lawḥ), you inscribe the writing onto the tablet with an iron stylus (mil). If it is on paper or leather, you write with a reed pen (kamish). When you cut the tip of the reed pen, you say three times, [I 12] and having said it, you recite the following noble verse, the third verse of Surah at-Talaq:

.And whoever puts his trust in God — He is sufficient for him) Indeed, God accomplishes His purpose; God has set a measure for all things.) You recite this. After cutting the tip of the reed pen, you take the pen in your hand and say:
(I have cut my pen for the sake of such-and-such a working.)
In place of "such-and-such," you say whatever your purpose actually is. If you recite the noble verse first, the working becomes more effective and more potent.

If the working you are performing is for love or attraction (mahabba), and the planetary natures of the maṭlūb (the object of the working) and the talib (the seeker, the one on whose behalf the working is done) are friendly to one another, you write both of their names. If their planets are enemies to one another, you write only the name of the maṭlūb, and do not write the name of the talib.

After these conditions, let us explain the calculation of abjad (the numerical alphabet), the elements (ʿanāṣir) of the twenty-eight letters, the luminous (nurani) and dark (zulmani) letters, the natures of the elements, their friendship and enmity with one another, the properties of the planets, their friendship and enmity, their letters, their incenses (bakhūr), and also their fortune (said)

and misfortune (nahis) and their exaltation (sheref). After that, let us clearly explain the properties of the zodiacal signs (burjh), their friendship and enmity, the mansions of the moon, in which sign the moon is found, and in which sign the sun is found — so that those who seek this science may understand it easily.
[I 13] About Abjad

Abjad table of letter-number values — eight rows read right to left, alternating a row of Arabic letters with a row giving each letter's numerical value, running from the units through the tens, hundreds and thousands. no labels. [I 13]
Concerning abjad, Hazrat Ali (may God be pleased with him) has said:
(Learn the rules of abjad, its numerical values, and the methods of its use, for through them many wondrous mysteries come to light.)
THE GREAT ABJAD (Abjad al-Kabir)
In the Abjad al-Kabir — the most widely used, and the original, principal abjad — the numbers run one by one from one (1) to ten (10). This is the Abjad al-Kabir (Great Abjad).

Abjad table with reduced letter values — rows alternate Arabic letters with their assigned numbers; the only word is "Sakit" ("fallen away, void"), marking letters to which no value is assigned. [I 14]
[I 14] THE LESSER ABJAD (Abjad Saghir)

This abjad is called Abjad Saghir (Lesser Abjad). This lesser abjad is derived from the greater abjad. If twelve (12) is subtracted, twelve at a time, from the numerical value of each letter in the Abjad al-Kabir, the number that remains is that letter's equivalent.

For example: the letter Lam has the value thirty in the Abjad Kabir. If we subtract twelve, twelve at a time, from this number, six remains. The equivalent of the letter Lam in the Abjad Saghir is six (6). The letter Ra has the value two hundred (200) in the Abjad Kabir. If we subtract twelve (12), twelve at a time, from this number, eight (8) remains. The equivalent of the letter Ra in the Abjad Saghir (Lesser Abjad) is eight (8).
This is the Abjad Saghir (Lesser Abjad):

In the Abjad Saghir, four letters are sakit (dropped, literally "fallen"). These four letters are Sin, Shīn, Khāʾ, and Ẓāʾ. If we subtract twelve, twelve at a time, from these letters' values in the Abjad Kabir, zero remains. For this reason these four letters are sakit.
Abjad table of expanded letter values — rows alternate Arabic letters with the numerical value of each letter's fully spelled-out name (alif written out = 111, and so on). no labels. [I 15]
[I 15] THE GREAT JUMMAL ABJAD (Abjad jummal kabīr)

The Great Jummal Abjad is calculated according to the numeric values of the letters' own names. For example: the letter Jīm is written and named "Jīm," which is made up of three letters. The sum of the numeric values of these three letters is (3 + 10 + 40 = 53). The letter Qāf is written and named "Qāf," which is likewise made up of three letters. The sum of the numeric values of these three letters is: Qāf 100, Alif 1, and the letter Fe 80, totaling 181.
The Great Abjad value of the letter Qāf is 181.

In the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Compassionate, and may God bless our master Muḥammad and his family and his Companions, and grant them peace.

A testimony of pre-eternity (azal)! From the light of this testimony the elect have scooped up knowledge — so understand that. And the everlasting ordering lies in the two testimonies conjoined with [the testimony of] the noble angels, those possessed of knowledge; this, then, is the testimony of everlastingness (abad). Whoever grasps the secret of these two testimonies beholds the two dominions; then I have entrusted to him the secret of connection with the unveilings (kashfiyyāt), and every configuration that conveys him to all the matters of wisdom.
And I ask of God, the Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm), that He make it an alms accepted before my intimate discourse [with

Him]; that He grant me the companionship of the spirit of His gladdening in my going to and fro and in my resting place; that He make the way plain to me and to you, and favour us and you with the lights of realization (taḥqīq). Truly this flash of Mercy (al-barqa al-raḥamūtiyya) and these shining, luminous suns are the ways of the gnostics, the highway of the veracious, and the very heart of those who set their course for the holy Presence of the Lord of the Worlds — God of the first and of the last, Lord of lords, who rends open the causes and lifts the veil, the Originator without any model, transcendent above genera and forms, the Everlasting who has never ceased and shall never cease to be qualified by the descriptions of perfection, perpetual in existence in pre-eternity, who raises up the celestial realms by His determining and His wisdom and spreads out the terrestrial realms by His power and His will. There is no god but He, the Great, the Most High (al-Kabīr al-Mutaʿāl), veiled behind the veils of the lights, hidden from all secrets, concealed from the pavilions of sight. He was inward with respect to His Essence in His pre-eternity, and became manifest through His attributes in His everlastingness; He made Himself openly known through His names in His sempiternity, and disclosed Himself through His acts in His duration. He is the First in pre-eternity, the Last in everlastingness, and the Manifest in sempiternity. He is exalted beyond substances and accidents, beyond parts and portions, and beyond acting for any purpose. The directions and the regions do not contain Him; the succession of the motions of the cycles does not wear Him away; the passing of night and day does not annihilate Him — glorified and exalted is He. Everything with Him is by measure; He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Most High.

And I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, who has no partner a testimony that accompanies the spirits with steadfastness in the intermediate states (barzakhiyyāt). He has known the full reckoning of His creation, the living and the dead; He has apportioned the provisions and the sustenance; He knows what has passed and what is to come, and He brings the dead to life after they have become crumbled remains. And I bear witness that our master Muḥammad is His servant and His Messenger, the sun of the religious community, the deliverer of [God's] servants from associationism (shirk) and from abasement, who set the sphere of the divine oneness (tawḥīd) turning by his summons. The crescent moons of religion took their light from the suns of his wisdom; the stars of error sank away at the sight of him; and the morning of those who affirm God's oneness broke bright through his felicity. May God bless him and his family and his Companions with the most excellent of enduring blessings, and may God, exalted is He, be well pleased with the Companions, the realizers, the veracious — may God be pleased with them all — with a blessing that conveys them to the highest ranks and the loftiest degrees. To proceed: the Truth has its guiding marks, and Reality has its order, and the spirits have an earnest concern for the divine gnoses. Excellence is a thing sought after, and the power to acquire it is a thing bestowed; felicity is conjoined with the suns of perfection; and everlasting life is pledged upon (marhūna bi-) the employment of the observances of the sacred Law. The highest of the degrees in ʿIlliyyūn are the degrees of the learned and of those who act; and the highest of them in degree and station is that of the guides, the realizers. There is no station in the religion of God for a scholar who gives no benefit, just as there is no existence of life for the reality of a soul that receives no benefit. And the furthest of people from felicity is he who makes light of the ordinances of the religious community and neglects the conditions [laid down by] the realizers among the people of the qibla.

Now, when I saw that each of the masters — those whose word has stood high, whose wisdom has spread abroad through the horizons, and whose blessing has extended over all created beings — had composed works upon the operative deployment (taṣrīf) of the names, upon the secrets of the letters, the litanies of remembrance, and the invocations; and when one whose affection was bound to me besought me to make plain to him the secret of what they had composed and the treasure of what they had laid up: then I answered him — while acknowledging my incapacity to comprehend the apprehensions of the forebears who have passed away and of the realizing, guiding imāms — and I hoped from God, through the offering of confession and of [acknowledged] wrongdoing, that He would supply me from the spirits of their spirits with a subtlety of succour, so that the utterance might accord with realization and be joined to the tongue of affirmation.

So I say — and in God is help sought: Know that the aim of the chapters of this book is that thereby there may be known the nobility of the names of God, exalted is He, and what God, exalted is He, has deposited in their sea of the various kinds of gems of wisdom and divine subtleties, and how the operative use of the names of the invocations is made, together with what follows upon them of the letters of the suras and the verses. I have set this book out in chapters, so that each chapter may point to what it encompasses and has enumerated of the subtle sciences by which one attains connection to the Lordly Presence without toil and without incurring hardship, and to what among them leads on to the desirable things of this world and to what is desired therein. And I have named this blessed and choice book — without peer, exalted in learning "The Sun of Gnosis and the Subtleties of Benefactions" because of what it holds within it of the subtleties of the operative deployments and the benefactions of the efficacious influences. It is therefore forbidden to anyone into whose hand this book of mine falls to show it to one who is not fit for it, or to divulge it to one who does not deserve it; for whenever he does that, God, exalted is He, will deprive him of its benefits, and its advantages and its blessing will be withheld from him. Beware of touching it while you are not in a state of purity. Do not read it save as one engaged in remembrance [of God], and do not put it to operative use save in that wherein God's good pleasure lies. Beware of anything other than obedience, lest you be stripped of its secret and denied its blessing; for it is the book of the friends of God (awliyāʾ), the righteous, the obedient, the aspirants, those who act, and those who yearn. So be chary of it, and relinquish nothing of it, little or much. Let your certainty be true and your faith in its realities firm: ((Deeds are only by intentions, and every man shall have only what he intended.)) And when an intention arises in you for one of the operations, then have faith in it and hold it true, in accordance with his saying — upon him be blessing and peace — ((Let none of you supplicate except while he is certain of being answered.)); and judge your operation to be sound, in accordance with his saying — upon him be blessing and peace — ((When one of you asks his Lord, let him be resolute in the asking, for there is none who can compel Him.)); and be certain of the answer, and judge your operation to be sound, in accordance with his saying — God bless him and grant him peace — ((One of you will be answered so long as he does not grow hasty and say: I have supplicated and I have not been answered.)) Beware of reckoning the answer slow in coming; rather, remain ever waiting and watching for its appearance.

This upright canon and straight path comprises forty chapters, each set out in detail, every chapter comprising meanings, indications, and symbols both hidden and manifest. So ponder them with your intellect.

I say and from God is help sought, and upon Him is reliance placed: the aims of those who seek [this knowledge] fall into two divisions, the worldly and the otherworldly, and each of the two is further divided into sections according to the purposes intended. People had discoursed upon the matching (muʿāraḍa) of awfāq, upon the observation of the planets, upon the ascetic disciplines (riyāḍāt), and upon the operations of talismans, before this book was composed and before there was any discussion of it. This is a broad science, one that many people have desired, worked with, and persevered in — especially any who have found some effect in it. So I wished to set over against that a description that runs in the manner of an occult property (khāṣṣa), within the direction taken by the practitioners of the science just mentioned, of
